text: Read the article by R. May entitled Uses and Abuses of Mathematics in Biology . How does this article illustrate the dangers of trusting models blindly? Do you find the arguments convincing?

Read at least three of the news articles below. Rapid Response Could Have Curbed Foot-and-Mouth Epidemic by Martin Enserink Disease control: Virtual plagues get real by V. Gewin African swine fever outbreak alarms wildlife biologists and veterinarians by Erik Stokstad U.K. expands kill zone for badgers in fight against bovine TB, sparking controversy by Erik Stokstad Italy’s olive crisis intensifies as deadly tree disease spreads by Alison Abbott Why computer simulations should replace animal testing for heart drugs , by Elisa Passini, Blanca Rodriguez, and Patricia Benito Could computer models be the key to better COVID vaccines? by Elie Dolgin OFF THE GRID: Computer models that forecast overloaded power lines are holding back U.S. solar and wind energy projects , by Dan Charles Then answer the following questions; include a discussion of the articles that you read (with proper references) in your argumentation. Do you believe mathematical models should be used to make decisions that impact people and society? Why or why not? What criteria do you think such models should satisfy, if they are to be used for policy-making purposes?

Assume you are an important business or government person, and that you have to make a decision that will influence the future of many people. Your decision relies on simulations of a mathematical model. What kind of questions would you ask the developers of the model, in order to help you in your decision-making process?

Read the article by N. Goldenfeld and L. Kadanoff, entitled Simple Lessons from Complexity . Summarize the main points of this paper and indicate which of the authors' conclusions you think one should especially keep in mind when developing a model.

Consider a set of data points in the plane $latex D =\{(X_i,Y_i),\ i=1,\dots n\},$ and a straight line of equation $latex y =a x + b.$ Define the distance $latex \delta$ between the data set $latex D$ and the set $latex F = \{(X_i,f(X_i)),\ i = 1, \dots n\}$ as $latex \delta = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (f(X_i)-Y_i)^2.$ Show that one can find a pair $latex (a, b)$ which minimizes the value of $latex \delta.$ This particular choice of parameters provides a linear fit, $latex y = a x + b,$ of the data set $latex D.$ This fitting technique is called the least squares method .

Using the least squares method (see Problem 5), find the straight line that best fits the following data points: (1,3.3), (2.5, 8), (4,13), (7,22), (8,25.5). Plot the line and the data points on the same graph. Is the fit satisfactory? Why or why not?

Browse the MATLAB documentation on curve fitting, and familiarize yourself with MATLAB's basic fitting interface. Create a set of data points close to the graphs of the following functions, and see if the fit proposed by MATLAB is satisfactory. What do you conclude? $latex f(x) = 3 x + 5.$ $latex f(x) = 7 x.$ $latex f(x) = \exp(3 x + 7).$ $latex f(x) = \exp(7 x).$
Find three different bell-shaped or pulse-like functions. How do you adjust their height? How do you adjust their width?

Find a monotone, differentiable function $latex f(x)$ defined on the real line, and such that $latex \lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = -6,$ $latex \lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = 3.$ Plot the function you found and check that it is monotonically increasing from -6 (as $latex x \to -\infty$) to 3 (as $latex x \to +\infty$).
Plot the function $latex f(t)=1/\cosh(b t)$ for various values of $latex b$. Describe in words the role of this parameter.
Plot the function $latex w(y) = e^{-|y|/R} \left(1 - \tanh (a y)\right)$ for different values of the parameters $latex R$ and $latex a$. Describe in words the role of each parameter.
How would you modify the model described in this chapter in order to take into account the presence of aisles or stairs in a stadium?

Read the articles by Farkas et al. entitled Mexican waves in an excitable medium and Human waves in stadiums .  Do you find their model convincing? Is all of the needed information actually included in the articles? Why or why not? Are the hypotheses made by the authors essential? Explain.

What are the similarities and differences between the model discussed in this chapter and a one-dimensional version of the detailed $latex n$-state model of Farkas et al. entitled Mexican waves in an excitable medium and Human waves in stadiums ? Justify your answer.

Show that $latex \theta(\tau) = C \cos(\tau + \phi),$ with $latex A, B \in \mathbb{R}$  can be written as  $latex \theta(\tau) = A \cos(\tau) + B \sin(\tau),$  with $latex C, \phi \in \mathbb{R}$ by expressing $latex A$ and $latex B$ in terms of $latex C$ and $latex \phi$.  Conversely, explain how you would find $latex C$ and $latex \phi$, knowing $latex A$ and $latex B$. Are $latex C$ and $latex \phi$ uniquely determined? Why or why not?

It is shown in the text that there exist solutions to Equation ( 3.8 ) which exhibit periodic oscillations. Write down an equation for the period $latex T$ of these oscillations, as an integral over the angle variable $latex \theta$. Your answer should depend on the energy $latex E$. Show that the period $latex T$ is an increasing function of the energy $latex E$. In other words, show that the period of the nonlinear pendulum increases with its amplitude.

Consider a one-dimensional frictionless spring-mass system, where the forces acting on the mass $latex m$ at position $latex x$ are the force of gravity $latex F_g = - m g$ with $latex g \gt 0$ constant, and the restoring force of the spring given by $latex F_r = - k (x - x_0)$, where $latex k \gt 0$ and $latex x_0$ are constant. Use Newton's law to write down an equation for the position $latex x$ of the mass. Re-scale the resulting equation. How many parameters can you get rid of? Show that the frictionless spring-mass system is conservative. Describe the dynamics of this system.

Consider a linear system of the form $latex \displaystyle \frac{d}{d t} \left(\begin{array}{c} x \cr y \end{array}\right) = \left( \begin{array}{cc} a & 0 \cr 0 & b \end{array} \right) \left(\begin{array}{c} x \cr y \end{array}\right),$  where $latex a \gt 0,\ b \lt 0.$  Give the general solution to this system. Sketch the phase plane of this system, paying particular attention to special trajectories. Can you tell in which direction the solution curves are traced out as time goes on? If so, add arrows to the trajectories you drew.
Sketch the phase plane in the vicinity of the following types of fixed points: A stable node. An unstable spiral. A center. A saddle point.
Describe the eigenvalues of the linearization of a system of dimension two in the vicinity of the following fixed points: A stable node. An unstable spiral. A center. A saddle point.

Find a 2 by 2 matrix $latex A$ whose entries are all non-zero, and such that the linear system $latex \dot X = A X$ has a fixed point of the following type at the origin: A stable node. An unstable spiral. A center. A saddle point. Check your answer with a phase plane analysis software, such as the Phase Plane App or equivalent software.

Explain how you would determine the nature (e.g. stable or unstable node or spiral, linear center or saddle point) of a fixed point $latex (x_0,y_0)$ of the two-dimensional differential system $latex \displaystyle \frac{d x}{d t} = F(x,y), \qquad \frac{d y}{d t} = G(x,y).$

Sketch the phase planes of the following dynamical systems. If the answer depends on the parameter(s) of the problem, all cases should be considered. Use the Phase Plane App or equivalent software to check your results. $latex \displaystyle \frac{d}{d t} \left(\begin{array}{c}x \cr y \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c}y \cr - x - c\, y \end{array}\right), \qquad c \gt 0$. $latex \displaystyle \frac{d}{d t} \left(\begin{array}{c}x \cr y \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c}y \cr x (x+1) (x-2) \end{array}\right)$. $latex \displaystyle \frac{d}{d t} \left(\begin{array}{c}x \cr y \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c}y \cr x (x+1) (x-2) - c\, y \end{array}\right), \qquad c \gt 0$. $latex \displaystyle \frac{d}{d t} \left(\begin{array}{c}x \cr y \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c} x (6 - 2 y) \cr y (x - 3) \end{array}\right)$. $latex \displaystyle \frac{d}{d t} \left(\begin{array}{c}x \cr y \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c} x (1 - x - 2 y) \cr y (1 - 3 x - y) / 2 \end{array}\right)$. $latex \displaystyle \frac{d}{d t} \left(\begin{array}{c}x \cr y \end{array}\right) = \left(\begin{array}{c} y \cr x -x^3 \end{array}\right)$.

Consider the van der Pol oscillator, $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \omega^2 x = \epsilon \frac{d x}{d t} (1 - x^2), \qquad \epsilon \ge 0.$  Describe the dynamics when $latex \epsilon=0$. What is the effect of the right-hand-side when $latex |x|$ is small? What is the effect of the right-hand-side when $latex |x|$ is much larger than $latex 1$? Based on your answers to the previous questions, explain what you expect to happen for intermediate values of $latex |x|$. Sketch the phase plane of the van der Pol oscillator. Check your answer with the Phase Plane App or equivalent software. Is the result surprising? Why or why not?

Consider the following differential equation, $latex \displaystyle \frac{d x}{d t} = \lambda x - \gamma x^3.$ What is the dimension of $latex \lambda$? What is the dimension of $latex \gamma$? Your answer should be in terms of the dimension of $latex x$, denoted by $latex [x]$. Let $latex t_0$ be a characteristic time scale for this problem. Define a dimensionless time variable $latex \tau = t / t_0$, and show that you can make a change of variable from $latex t$ to $latex \tau$, to "remove" the parameter $latex \lambda$. Can you find a change of variable that would allow you to remove $latex \gamma$ as well?

The force of gravity between two bodies of mass $latex m_1$ and $latex m_2$ has intensity $latex \displaystyle F = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2},$ where $latex r$ is the distance between the centers of mass of the two bodies, and $latex G$ is the gravitational constant. Use this formula to show that for an object of mass $latex m$ at the surface of the Earth, one can approximate the force $latex F$ by $latex F \simeq m g$, where the acceleration of gravity $latex g$ is constant. Express $latex g$ in terms of $latex G$, the mass $latex M$ of the Earth, and the radius $latex R$ of the Earth.

Consider a smooth function $latex f(x)$, and its Taylor expansion near $latex x = x_0$, $latex \displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{i = 0}^n f^{(i)}(x_0) \frac{(x - x_0)^i}{i !} + f^{(n+1)}(\bar x) \frac{(x - x_0)^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}, \qquad (3.20)$  where $latex \bar x \in [x_0,x]$. Let $latex E_n(x)$ be the error made by approximating $latex f$ with its Taylor expansion truncated to order $latex n$,  $latex \displaystyle E_n(x) = f(x) - \sum_{i = 0}^n f^{(i)}(x_0) \frac{(x - x_0)^i}{i !} .$  Use Equation (3.20) above to write the Taylor expansion of $latex f(x) = \cos(x)$, near $latex x_0 = 0$ to order $latex n = 5$. Find a condition on $latex |x|$ which ensures that $latex \vert E_5(x) \vert \lt 0.05$. Use a calculator or MATLAB to check your answer to the previous question.

Consider the following model $latex \displaystyle \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \mu u + \alpha \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} - \beta u^3, \qquad u \in \mathbb{R}, \quad \alpha, \beta \gt 0.$  What are the dimensions of the parameters $latex \alpha$, $latex \beta$ and $latex \mu$? Write $latex [u]$ for the dimension of $latex u$. How many relevant parameters does this model have? Explain.

Consider the second order differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \frac{d V}{d x} = 0,$ where $latex V(x)$ is a smooth potential. Re-write this second order equation as a first-order system. Find the fixed points of the first-order system and show that they correspond to critical points of $latex V$. Find the linearized system about an arbitrary fixed point and show that maxima of $latex V$ correspond to saddle points and minima of $latex V$ to linear centers.

Consider the dynamical system $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \frac{d V}{d x} = 0,$ where $latex V(x)$ is a smooth function. Assume that $latex (x_0, 0)$ is a saddle point of the corresponding first-order system of differential equations. Find an equation describing the trajectories in the associated phase plane near the fixed point $latex (x_0, 0)$.

Consider the dynamical system $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \frac{d V}{d x} = 0,$ where $latex V(x)$ is a smooth function.  Show that, in the phase plane of coordinates $latex \left(x,\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right)$, trajectories with energy $latex E$ such that $latex \min(V) \lt E \lt \max(V)$ (where $latex \min(V)$ and/or $latex \max(V)$ may be infinite depending on the potential $latex V$) cross the $latex x$-axis. In addition, show that they have a vertical tangent at points of crossing where $latex \displaystyle \frac{d V}{d x} \ne 0$.

Sketch the phase plane associated with the differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \frac{d V}{d x}=0,$ where the potential $latex V(x)$ has the shape given below. Only the portion of the graph of $latex V(x)$ near its minimum is shown. You may assume that the trends suggested by the picture continue outside of the plot area, i.e. that $latex \displaystyle \lim_{x \to - \infty} V(x) = \lim_{x \to + \infty} V(x) = + \infty.$    Image description : A graph of a potential energy function showing a single, smooth, U-shaped curve (like a slightly deformed parabola) with a minimum at the center. The curve opens upward and rises toward infinity on both the left and right sides. An arrow below the curve indicates the horizontal axis is $latex x$.

Sketch the phase plane associated with the differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \frac{d V}{d x} = 0,$ where the potential $latex V(x)$ has the shape given below. Only the portion of the graph of $latex V(x)$ near its extrema is shown. You may assume that the trends suggested by the picture continue outside of the plot area, i.e. that $latex \displaystyle \lim_{x \to - \infty} V(x) = \lim_{x \to + \infty} V(x) = + \infty.$    Image description : A graph of a potential energy function featuring two distinct valleys (local minima) separated by a single central peak (local maximum). The valley on the left is deeper than the valley on the right. An arrow labeled $latex x$ indicates the horizontal axis. The curve rises sharply at both the far left and far right ends.

Sketch the phase plane associated with the differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \frac{d V}{d x} = 0,$ where the potential $latex V(x)$ has the shape given below. Only the portion of the graph of $latex V(x)$ near its extrema is shown. You may assume that the trends suggested by the picture continue outside of the plot area, i.e. that $latex \displaystyle \lim_{x \to - \infty} V(x) = + \infty, \quad \lim_{x \to + \infty} V(x) = \,- \infty.$    Image description : A graph of a potential energy function showing a smooth curve with one local minimum (a valley) and one local maximum (a peak). An arrow below the curve indicates the horizontal axis is $x$. The curve descends from the left into the valley, rises to the peak, and then descends sharply toward the right.

Sketch the phase plane associated with the differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 x}{d t^2} + \frac{d V}{d x} = 0,$ where the potential $latex V(x)$ has the shape given below. Only the portion of the graph of $latex V(x)$ near its extrema is shown. You may assume that the trends suggested by the picture continue outside of the plot area, i.e. that $latex \displaystyle \lim_{x \to - \infty} V(x) = \,- \infty, \quad \lim_{x \to + \infty} V(x) = + \infty.$    Image description : A graph of a potential energy function featuring two peaks (local maxima) and two distinct valleys (local minima). The curve starts by rising to a small peak on the left, dips into a shallow valley, rises to a taller central peak, dips into a much deeper valley on the right, and finally rises sharply toward infinity. An arrow labeled $latex x$ indicates the horizontal axis.

u$. Let $latex U$ be a characteristic velocity, and $latex l$ a characteristic length. Re-write the Navier-Stokes equation in terms of these new variables. Show that if you now re-scale time and introduce dimensionless versions of $latex p$ and $latex \vec F$, then the dimensionless Navier-Stokes equation involves only one parameter, $latex Re = U l / 
u$. This parameter is called the Reynolds number .

Consider Equations ( 4.5 ). Use these equations to determine the dimension of $latex \omega_\alpha$, where $latex \alpha$ is each of $latex y,\,n$ and $latex p$. Relate the dimension of $latex I_\alpha$ to that of $latex N_\alpha$. Given that a torque is of the form $latex \vec N = \vec r \times \vec f$ where $latex \vec r$ is a position vector and $latex \vec f$ a force, find the dimension of $latex N_\alpha$. Use the above to find the dimension of $latex I_\alpha$. Does this agree with the definition $latex I_\alpha \equiv \int ||\vec r||^2 \rho\,dV,$ where $latex \rho$ is a density and $latex dV$ is a volume element?

This problem is based on the 2003 article by L. Bocquet. Consider Equation ( 4.11 ), and assume that the stone has a square shape. Show that $latex S_{im} = a |z| / \sin(\theta)$. Using the expression for $latex S_{im}$, show that Equation ( 4.11 ) becomes a linear differential equation for $latex z$. Find the general solution this ordinary differential equation. Apply the boundary conditions and show that $latex z(t)$ is given by  $latex \displaystyle z(t) = \frac{-g}{\omega_0^2} + \frac{g}{\omega_0^2} \cos(\omega_0 t) + \frac{v_z(0)}{\omega_0} \sin(\omega_0 t),$  $latex \displaystyle \text{where } \qquad \omega_0^2 = \frac{\left(C_l \cos(\theta)-C_f \sin(\theta)\right) \rho_w v_x(0)^2 a}{2 M \sin(\theta)}$.

This problem is based on the 2003 article by L. Bocquet. The dynamics of the immersed edge of a square stone during a collision phase is described by (see Problem 2) $latex \displaystyle z(t) = \frac{-g}{\omega_0^2} + \frac{g}{\omega_0^2} \cos(\omega_0 t) + \frac{v_z(0)}{\omega_0} \sin(\omega_0 t),$ where $latex \displaystyle \omega_0^2 = \frac{\left(C_l \cos(\theta)-C_f \sin(\theta)\right) \rho_w v_x(0)^2 a}{2 M \sin(\theta)}.$  Use this expression to show that the edge of the stone reaches a depth $latex |z_m|$, given by $latex z_m = - \frac{g}{\omega_0^2} \left[1+\sqrt{1+\frac{\omega_0^2 v_z(0)^2}{g^2}}\right].$ What is the condition on $latex z$ for the stone to be completely immersed? Show that the stone will not be completely immersed during a collision phase if $latex \displaystyle v_x(0)^2 > \frac{4 M g}{C \rho_w a^2} \left[1 - \frac{2 \tan^2 \beta \, M}{a^3 C \rho_w \sin(\theta)}\right]^{-1}, \quad C = C_l \cos(\theta)-C_f \sin(\theta).$

This problem is based on the 2003 article by L. Bocquet. Using Euler's equations of motion ( 4.5 ), together with the appropriate expressions for the lift force applied to stone during the collision phase, derive Equation (20) of the 2003 article by L. Bocquet, $latex \displaystyle \frac{d^2 \theta}{d t^2} + \frac{J_0 - J_1}{J_1} (\theta - \theta(0)) = \frac{{\mathcal M}_\theta}{J_1},$ where $latex {\mathcal M}_\theta$ is the projection on the $latex \vec y$ axis of the torque exerted by the water on the stone.

Assume that a population grows according to $latex \displaystyle N(t+1) = \kappa N(t), \kappa > 1.$ How long does it take to double the number of individuals? Estimate the value of $latex \kappa$ from Figure 5.1, which shows the number of Red-tailed Hawks in the United States as a function of time. Is your estimate of $latex \kappa$ in reasonable agreement with the value $latex \kappa = 1.025$ inferred from Figure 5.3?

Consider the continuous model $latex \displaystyle \frac{d N}{d t} = r N, r > 0.$ How long does it take to double $latex N$? If this model is an approximation of a difference equation of the form $latex N(t + \Delta t) = \kappa N(t),$ what is the relationship between $latex \kappa$ and $latex r$? How long does it take for a system described by the discrete model to double its population? Is the discrete model faster or slower than its continuous approximation?

Consider the continuous model $latex \displaystyle \frac{dN}{dt} = r(N) N,$ where $latex r(N)$ is a linear function of $latex N$: $latex r(N) = a N + b$. What should the signs of $latex a$ and $latex b$ be if one wants the population to grow for small values of $latex N$ and saturate at large values of $latex N$? What changes of variables should you make to turn this model into Equation ( 5.5 )?

Find the non-trivial fixed point of the logistic map $latex x_{n+1} = a x_n (1 - x_n) \equiv f(x_n), 0 \lt a \lt 4.$  Show that this fixed point becomes unstable when $latex a > 3$. Show that as soon as this fixed point becomes unstable, a period-two cycle of the map starts to exist. Hint : look for fixed points of $latex f^2$. Find the value of $latex a$ at which this period-two cycle becomes unstable. Check your answer against the bifurcation diagram of Figure 5.6.

Solve the difference equation $latex \displaystyle X(t + 1) = \left(\begin{array}{cc} 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 3 \end{array}\right) X(t)$, where $latex X(t)$ has two components: $latex \displaystyle X(t) = \left(\begin{array}{c} x(t) \\ y(t) \end{array}\right).$ Assume the initial conditions are $latex x(0)=1$ and $latex y(0) = 0.$
Consider the differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d x}{d t} = x (x - 1) (x - 2).$ What are the fixed point of the dynamics? Are they stable or unstable?
Consider the differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d x}{d t} = x^2 (x-1).$ What are the fixed point of the dynamics? Are they stable or unstable?

Consider the differential equation $latex \displaystyle \frac{d x}{d t} = a + x^2 (x-1) \equiv f(x), a \in \mathbb{R}.$ Plot $latex f(x)$ as a function of $latex x$. What happens as $latex a$ changes? Without performing any calculation, sketch the behavior of the fixed points as a function of $latex a$. Indicate the stability of each fixed point on the bifurcation diagram of question (2). Assign a value of +1 to each stable fixed point and a value of -1 to each unstable fixed point. For each value of $latex a$, define a function $latex g(a)$ as the sum of indices associated with the fixed points existing for this particular value of $latex a$. Sketch the graph of $latex g$ as a function of $latex a$. What do you observe?

Consider a population model where the age $latex a$ is a continuous independent variable. Define the age distribution $latex M(a,t)$ such that the number of individuals between age $latex a_1$ and age $latex a_2$ at time $latex t$ is given by $latex \int_{a_1}^{a_2} M(a,t) d a.$ Show that the dynamics of $latex M$ is described by the following partial differential equation, known as the McKendrick or von Foerster partial differential equation, $latex \displaystyle \frac{\partial M}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial M}{\partial a} = - d(a) M,$ where the mortality function $latex d(a)$ represents the per capita death rate of individuals of age $latex a$.
Use the method of characteristics to solve the McKendrick partial differential equation derived in Problem 9.

Consider the LPA model described in this chapter. What are the dimensions of the parameters ($latex b$, $latex c_{ea}$, $latex c_{el}$, $latex c_{pa}$, $latex d_a$, $latex d_l$) appearing in this model?

Write a model describing a situation analogous to that of the LPA model (with cannibalism), but such that the time for a pupa to become an adult is twice as long as the time it takes for a larva to pupate.

Write a model describing a population with two subgroups, juvenile and adults, in which adults eat some of their own eggs. You can use an exponential term similar to that appearing in the LPA model to describe cannibalism.

Consider the following model, $latex \displaystyle \left\{\begin{array}{l} J(t + \Delta t)=b A(t) \exp\left(- c A(t)\right),\\ A(t + \Delta t)=(1 - d_J) J(t) + (1 - d_A) A(t), \end{array}\right.$ where $latex b$, $latex d_J$ and $latex d_A$ are positive parameters. Describe in words a situation modeled by the above equations. Under what condition is there a non-trivial fixed point for this model? What is the biological significance of this condition? Discuss the stability of the fixed points of this model.

Read the article by R. The goal of this problem is to explore global changes in the population of the United States. The U.S. Census Bureau maintains a file ( popclockest.txt ) containing national population estimates between 1900 and 1999. Import this data set into MATLAB or EXCEL. Then answer the following questions. Plot the U.S. population as a function of time. What do you conclude? Can the growth of the U.S. population be modeled by a simple evolution equation of the form $latex N(t+1) = (1+R) N(t)$, where $latex t$ is in years? Why or why not? If so, estimate $latex R$. Post-census population estimates are obtained as described on the U.S. Census Bureau methodology page (see for instance the methodology file for the 2021 vintage ). Explain the main formula given in the Overview section of this article. Given the following estimates[footnote]Downloaded in 2005 from a now decommissioned US Census Bureau web page (https://www.census.gov/popest/datasets.html)[/footnote] find the population of the U.S. in 2004: Population in 2001: 285,102,075. Births, deaths, and net international immigration: 2001-2002: 4,006,985; 2,429,999; 1,262,159. 2002-2003: 4,055,469; 2,432,874; 1,225,161. 2003-2004: 4,099,399; 2,453,984; 1,221,013.

The goal of this section is to explore the evolution of the population of the United States using different age groups. Population estimates by five-year age groups from 2010 to 2019 can be obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau web site (each year has its own table). Use the age distributions that you just plotted to define larger age groups that can be used in a simplified model. Using recent birth and death rates estimates, as published by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention, create a model to predict the population in the age groups you defined, taking the 2010 data as initial condition. You may want to start with Figures 2 and 3 of the birth and deaths documents, respectively. There are also tables at the end that may be of use. Use your model to predict the population in each age group in 2050. What do you conclude? Discuss the limitations of your model.
